text: Formulation With compressed sensing, we aim to create a measurement vector much smaller than the original signal by randomly sampling the original vector and reconstructing with the given information. Formulation of the measurement vector is given by equation 1. 𝑦 = 𝐶𝑠 (1) where y is the measurement vector of dimension M, s is the original one-dimensional signal M×1 N×1 of dimension N, and C is a random sensing matrix. We are able to decompose the signal M×N vector s. s = Ψ x (2) 3 In this formulation, Ψ is some basis matrix dependent on the domain the signal is N×N sparse in, and x is some sparse vector. In these cases, a Fourier basis (such as a discrete cosine transform matrix) would be used as the sensing matrix Ψ and vector x would consist of the sparse Fourier coefficients retrieved from a Fast Fourier Transform (FFT)1. For similar reasonings, it is also possible to use a wavelet basis8. For demonstrative purposes, Figures 2 and 3 show the data from location 1 in the Fourier domain and wavelet domain respectively; Figure 2: Discrete Fourier Transform of data set from Location 1 calculated via FFT. both depict dense (non-sparse) data that cannot be used for compressed sensing. When using compressed sensing, the number of measurements in the y vector (M) can vary, though a good value is bounded in both directions. The measurement vector should be less than the total measurements in the original signal (N). It is also known that M should follow O(K⋅log (N/K)) where K is the number of 2 non-zero values in the original dataset 1.
